claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength compared with other high-entropy alloys.
The low hardness and strength are governed by the absence of significant lattice distortion or second-phase precipitates.
Large atomic-size mismatches and nanoscale obstacles impede dislocation motion.
Freer dislocation glide promotes extensive plastic deformation and machinability.
The absence of dislocation barriers limits work hardening, hardness, and yield strength.
The proposed initial material is an equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with minimal chemical ordering and nanoprecipitates.
A slight compositional adjustment or aging treatment can introduce nanoscale precipitates or enhanced lattice distortion.
Atomic-size and electronegativity differences govern the magnitude of lattice distortion.
The constituent elements have nearly similar atomic radii.
Nearly similar atomic radii and low chemical ordering produce minimal lattice distortion in the homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Minimal lattice distortion provides few obstacles to dislocation motion.
Dislocation motion in the initial alloy occurs predominantly by easy glide and may be dominated by edge dislocations.
Introducing nanoscale inhomogeneities will impede dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation glide will increase strength and hardness while reducing ductility.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, a precipitate-forming or distortion-enhancing treatment should increase hardness and yield strength.
The predicted increase in hardness and yield strength should be accompanied by reduced ductility.
Simple homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi has excellent plasticity and machinability.
Chemical ordering or preexisting precipitates can already provide significant strengthening.
Extreme temperature or strain rate can alter the operative dislocation mechanisms.
